overview: Babur founded the Mughal dynasty in 1526. His successors built a major South Asian empire through warfare, alliances and administration, ruling peoples with many languages and religions. The map’s 1526 to 1857 record uses only a few broad outlines from 1530 to 1783; these cannot show every contested frontier, the interruption under the Sur rulers, or later regional independence.

periods.title: Babur and Humayun
periods.summary: Babur established the dynasty; Humayun then lost its Indian territories to Sher Shah Suri.

periods.title: An interrupted empire
periods.summary: The Sur dynasty displaced Mughal rule in northern India; Humayun eventually recovered Delhi and Agra.

periods.title: Restoration and Akbar’s expansion
periods.summary: Akbar consolidated government and extended rule across northern and central India.

periods.title: Jahangir and Shah Jahan
periods.summary: Imperial patronage supported painting, books and major architectural projects.

periods.title: Aurangzeb’s reign
periods.summary: Aurangzeb seized power from his father Shah Jahan; imperial patronage and court priorities changed.

periods.title: Weaker emperors, regional centers
periods.summary: The 1739 sack of Delhi accelerated disruption; nineteenth-century emperors survived under British protection.

periods.title: The last court overthrown
periods.summary: British forces retook Delhi during the uprising; the emperor’s capture ended the functioning Mughal court.

items.text: Akbar’s conquests included Gujarat, whose trading cities gave the empire access to the Arabian Sea. His power rested on a strong administrative system as well as armies. Ports and commercial routes helped connect the inland court with distant markets.

Akbar invited scholars of several religions to court discussions, including Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians. These meetings belonged to a particular ruler’s intellectual and political program; Mughal religious policies changed across reigns.

The court could travel as a vast tented settlement containing royal women, nobles, servants and followers. Under Jahangir, two sets of tents allowed the next stopping place to be prepared before the travelers arrived. Moving house could mean moving a whole temporary neighborhood.

Agriculture supplied most imperial revenue. Village cultivators faced assessors, collectors and record keepers seeking the state’s share, while crops grown for sale connected villages to towns. Palaces depended on work far beyond their walls.

Babur described irrigation near Lahore and Dipalpur: a bullock turned geared wheels that lifted a circulating chain of pitchers from a well. The pitchers emptied into a trough carrying water onward. This was a machine he observed in use, not an invention credited to the emperor.

Rural women worked in fields and crafts: sowing, weeding, processing harvested grain, spinning and preparing clay for pottery. Household production drew on the labor of women and men. The seclusion associated with elite royal women cannot describe all families across the empire.

Documents from Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra preserve women’s complaints to village councils about husbands neglecting wives and children. The records often omit the petitioner’s own name, identifying her through a male relative. Family disputes survive, but the archive does not give everyone an equal voice.

Gulbadan Begum, Babur’s daughter and Akbar’s aunt, wrote a Persian prose chronicle that recorded women’s experiences and family relationships. She also led royal women on a pilgrimage to Arabia and stayed there for years. The household included travelers, advisers and authors, not simply people waiting silently behind palace walls.

Lahore’s Shahi Hammam, built in 1634, was a public bathhouse. Excavators uncovered furnaces, drainage and a heating network: hot air and smoke warmed the floors while heated water reached the bathing rooms. A comfortable bath required fuel, maintenance and some serious work underneath the floor.

Nearby, the Wazir Khan Mosque complex built in 1634 to 1635 included entrance shops intended for calligraphers and bookbinders. Worship, skilled work and the city’s book trade occupied adjoining spaces. Making a manuscript involved more people than the person whose words appeared on its pages.

A painting made at Lahore around 1595 shows boys reading in a school courtyard. A teacher works with a pupil on a carpeted platform while other students read alone or with tutors. Ascribed to Khem Karan, it illustrates a treatise on ethics: a carefully composed view of education rather than a classroom photograph.

After becoming emperor in 1605, Jahangir recorded an order calling for free hospitals and the appointment of physicians in the empire’s major cities. It expresses a royal commitment to care, but an order alone cannot establish how fully services reached patients. His memoir records what the ruler wanted to proclaim.

Mansur’s painting of two vultures, made around 1615 to 1620, distinguishes the birds through their forms and finely shaded feathers. The Met describes them as ornithologically accurate, while identifying the rocky setting as imagined. Close observation and artistic arrangement could share the same page.

The royal book workshops brought together calligraphers, painters and bookbinders. In the Akbarnama manuscript now at the V&A, small inscriptions identify different hands: one artist designed a picture and another applied its colors, sometimes with a specialist adding portraits. A celebrated page could be a team project.

sections.title: Objects and words to look for

items.text: The Taj Mahal at Agra commemorates Mumtaz Mahal, Shah Jahan’s wife. Work began in 1632; the mausoleum was completed in 1648 and the wider complex by 1653. Craftspeople combined white marble, carved ornament and colored stone inlay. Its garden, riverfront position and carefully arranged buildings work together as a designed landscape.

A red sandstone window screen at the Met dates to the later sixteenth century. Its pierced geometry cast moving patterns across a room as daylight changed. Weathering on one side suggests an exterior window. Stone could make a surprisingly delicate filter for light.

Jahangir’s inkpot, dated 1618 to 1619, was made from nephrite jade and gold. Its broad, heavy form made it difficult to knock over. Even luxurious writing equipment had a practical job: keeping the ink inside the pot was a useful beginning.

A Persian inscription on a portrait of Jahangir holding his father Akbar’s picture includes “عمل نادر الزمان,” meaning “painted by Nadir al-Zaman.” The Louvre dates the painting to 1600 to 1615 and identifies that artist as Abu al-Hasan. This short sample follows the museum’s transcription of the words on Akbar’s green globe.

As imperial workshops contracted, painters sought patrons in other courts, including Bikaner, Bundi, Lucknow and Murshidabad. After Nadir Shah’s devastating raid on Delhi in 1739, dispersal intensified. Political weakening could uproot skilled people while helping artistic practices develop in new regional settings.

ending.text: British forces captured Delhi in 1857 and dismantled the last Mughal court. Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried and exiled to Burma in 1858, when Crown rule replaced Company government. The dynasty’s end did not end South Asian communities or Mughal artistic traditions, which had already spread to regional patrons.
